sections.heading: What is the Merge Intervals Pattern?
sections.content: An interval is a range with a start and an end, such as [1, 5]. The Merge Intervals pattern deals with overlapping, adjacent or conflicting ranges. The key move is almost always the same: sort the intervals by start time, then scan once and compare each interval with the previous one. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan costs O(n).

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Merge overlapping intervals into one
Insert a new interval into a sorted list
Check if any meetings overlap (can a person attend all?)
Find the minimum number of rooms or resources needed
Find free time or gaps between intervals
Find the intersection of two interval lists
Remove the minimum number of intervals to avoid overlaps
Keywords: meetings, schedule, ranges, overlap, calendar, merge, booking

Decide About Touching Intervals
sections.content: Always ask whether [1, 3] and [3, 5] overlap. In Merge Intervals problems they usually do, so they become [1, 5]. In Meeting Rooms problems they usually do not, because one meeting ends exactly when the next begins. This one decision changes < to <= in your code.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to sort the intervals first
Using < instead of <= (or the other way) when touching intervals should merge
Not taking maxOf of the ends when merging: [1, 10] and [2, 5] should stay [1, 10]
Sorting by start when the greedy needs sorting by end
Forgetting to add the last interval after the loop in the merge template
Mutating the input array when the problem expects it unchanged
Subtracting values in a comparator, which can overflow (use compareBy or Integer.compare)

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Sort by start time to merge or detect overlap in one pass
Two intervals overlap when a.start <= b.end and b.start <= a.end
Merged interval is [min of starts, max of ends]
Sort by end time for greedy 'keep the most intervals' problems
Use a min heap or sweep line to count simultaneous intervals
Always decide how touching intervals such as [1, 3] and [3, 5] are treated
